issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment defines a safe pretraining-side proxy suite for competencies surfaced by Artificial Analysis-style model comparisons without adding held-out benchmark items to regular PPL tracking. The thread started with a broad mapping from AA tasks to existing Marin slices, then corrected course after a benchmark-leak audit: exact AA, HLE, GPQA, AIME/MATH, LiveCodeBench, IFBench, and similar test items should not become core tracking data. The current recommendation is to use non-benchmark or train/dev validation distributions, attach `ppl_fidelity` to each metric/rendering claim, and treat low-fidelity behaviors such as abstention, instruction following, long-context retrieval, and agentic state tracking as needing paired/discrimination or non-PPL companion metrics. Follow-up subissues #5823-#5829 split the work by competency area.

### Helpful links
- Benchmark-leak audit and replacement guidance: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5819#issuecomment-4483211940
- Competency subissues created from this design: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5819#issuecomment-4483255377
- Taxonomy refinement proposal: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5819#issuecomment-4505459965
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Identify a small text-only pretraining tracking suite that acts as an early, cheap proxy for the competencies stressed by Artificial Analysis-style model comparisons, without using the actual held-out benchmark items. Artificial Analysis' text-only index emphasizes agents, coding, general knowledge, scientific reasoning, long-context use, professional work, and instruction following, with multilingual tracked separately.

The goal is not to claim that raw perplexity replaces pass@1, instruction-following evals, or truthfulness evals. The goal is to catch data, tokenizer, format, and target-likelihood gaps during training on distributions that plausibly support those downstream competencies.

Current useful coverage includes Paloma, Uncheatable, FineWeb2 multilingual, Stack v2/code slices, structured tables, LM-eval bridge canaries, formal methods, bio/chem notation, MCQA train/dev slices, long-context slices, and LIMA/BookSum-style target-only slices. Remaining gaps include generated math, scientific/technical reasoning targets, instruction-following text, agentic coding/debugging traces, professional-document domains, and factual/evidential reasoning prerequisites.

## Scope and non-goals

Build a `text_comparison_core` bundle and candidate additions that track AA-like competencies while avoiding benchmark-maxxing.

This issue is about pretraining proxies where those proxies make sense. Some downstream AA behaviors may not have faithful pretraining PPL proxies. Truthfulness, hallucination robustness, and abstention are explicitly deferred as post-training or non-PPL evaluation targets. For pretraining, we should track prerequisites instead: factual recall, evidence-conditioned claim likelihood, contradiction sensitivity, source-conditioned answer likelihood, and long-context source use.

`ppl_fidelity` should be attached to a competency/metric/rendering claim, not to a dataset in isolation. A dataset can support multiple metrics with different fidelity: raw text PPL may measure domain familiarity, target-only likelihood may measure evidence use, paired correct-vs-distractor likelihood may measure discrimination, and abstention likelihood may still have low fidelity unless we explicitly train or evaluate calibration.

The coverage map should be sparse but intentional. We do not need to fill every capability x domain x surface cell; we need enough high-value intersections to notice when training is failing along an AA-relevant axis.

## Candidate tracking set

Initial recommended regular tracking set: Paloma core (`c4_en`, `wikitext_103`, `m2d2_s2orc`, `m2d2_wikipedia`, `dolma_100_programing_languages`), Uncheatable knowledge/code/science (`wikipedia_english`, `bbc_news`, `arxiv_physics`, `arxiv_computer_science`, `github_python`, `github_cpp`), LM-eval bridge canaries (`mmlu_auxiliary_train`, `gsm8k_train`), MCQA train/dev slices (ARC, OpenBookQA, CommonsenseQA, SciQ, QASC, RACE), structured tables (`totto`, `gittables`, `wikitablequestions`), selected FineWeb2 languages, long-context public-doc/QA/summarization slices, and `formal_methods/smt_lib`.

Candidate additions should be distributional or train/dev/non-benchmark surrogates: generated math templates and open math-prose derived QA; CI logs, diffs, issue-to-patch traces, Stack v2/code ecosystem, and #4963/#5248-style code slices for agentic coding; generated instruction-following transformations by constraint family; long public reports/legal/academic documents with synthetic QA/span reconstruction; professional documents such as SEC filings, contracts/law, patents, medical/regulatory text, and reports; and Wikipedia/Wikidata-derived factual cloze plus evidence-conditioned claim/contradiction tasks.

Core rule: do not add actual AA component items, GPQA/HLE/AIME/MATH/MMLU-Pro/IFBench/LiveCodeBench/SciCode exact questions, or near-duplicates as regular PPL tracking data. Exact benchmark-derived PPL, if ever used, should be opt-in diagnostic only, clearly labeled, and excluded from training-run core dashboards.

## Competency coverage targets

* General language and broad knowledge: Paloma, Uncheatable, Wikipedia/news, selected factual cloze.
* MCQA and answer-likelihood competence: MMLU auxiliary_train as a small canary plus ARC/OpenBookQA/CommonsenseQA/SciQ/QASC/RACE train/dev; prefer answer-text and paired-distractor likelihood where possible.
* Math and numeric reasoning: GSM8K train as a canary, generated math templates, numeric reasoning probes, and open math-prose derived QA.
* Scientific and technical reasoning: arXiv/S2ORC/PubMed-style text, bio/chem notation, formal-methods slices, MedQA/MedMCQA/PubMedQA train/dev if license-compatible, and generated source-grounded science tasks.
* Coding and debugging: Stack v2/code ecosystem, GitHub code, CI logs, shell transcripts, diffs, issue-to-patch traces, and unit-test-to-solution traces.
* Instruction following and format control: generated transformations by constraint family, structured outputs, counting/formatting constraints, and chat/instruction tuning corpora used as target-only likelihood canaries.
* Long-context reading and retrieval: long public reports/legal/academic/government documents, answer-span reconstruction, source-conditioned QA, BookSum-style summarization, and QASPER/NarrativeQA-style target-only slices.
* Professional-document competence: SEC/financial disclosures, contracts and law, medical/regulatory documents, patents, reports, memos, and spreadsheets-as-text.
* Multilingual text competence: selected FineWeb2 languages, optionally train/dev multilingual QA or MCQA sources that are not AA items.
* Factual/evidential reasoning prerequisites: factual recall, evidence-conditioned claim likelihood, contradiction sensitivity, and source-conditioned answer likelihood. Truthfulness, hallucination robustness, and abstention behavior remain deferred to post-training or non-PPL evaluation.

## Links

* Artificial Analysis methodology: https://artificialanalysis.ai/methodology/intelligence-benchmarking
* Perplexity workflow docs PR: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5803
* Anthropic calibration/self-knowledge paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221

## Results

Open. First pass should classify existing slices into AA-like competencies, decide which additions belong in regular training tracking versus archival diagnostics, and file implementation issues or PRs for the chosen non-benchmark validation datasets. The classification should record the competency, domain, surface/rendering, intended metric, expected `ppl_fidelity`, role (`headline`, `canary`, or `diagnostic`), and expected scaling regime where known.

| AA eval | What AA measures | Current Marin PPL surrogate(s) | Sufficiency | What to add |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GDPval-AA | Real-world knowledge work with professional deliverables and file outputs | Weak proxies: `structured_text/{totto,gittables,wikitablequestions}`, raw web/markup slices, package metadata | Insufficient | Text-only GDPval task prompts plus reference-doc/context text; supervised target spans for expected summaries, tables, code, or document snippets where available |
| tau2-Bench Telecom | Agent-user simulation, tool/state tracking, telecom workflows | Weak proxies: service logs, machine records, structured records if included in dashboard | Insufficient | tau2 conversation/state/action transcripts as supervised target-only next-action or final-state slices |
| Terminal-Bench Hard | Terminal-based task execution and software/sysadmin workflows | `uncheatable_eval/github_{python,cpp}`, Stack v2, `synthetic_patch_diff_ppl`, package metadata, shell/config/code slices | Partial for surface familiarity, insufficient for task success | terminal task prompt -> solution script/patch/log target slices; failing-test-to-patch traces |
| SciCode | Scientific Python coding with domain background | `uncheatable_eval/arxiv_{physics,computer_science}`, `formal_methods/*`, `bio_chem/*`, `github_python` | Partial | SciCode prompt/background -> canonical code or solution target-only slice |
| AA-LCR | Long-context reasoning over ~100k-token document sets | Very weak; current scoring defaults are short (`max_eval_length` around 4k, doc cap around 32KiB) | Insufficient | Long-context PPL mode at 32k/64k first; long reports/legal/academic docs plus answer-span target-only QA |
| AA-Omniscience | Factual answer accuracy plus hallucination/abstention | `paloma/wikitext_103`, `paloma/m2d2_wikipedia_unsplit`, `uncheatable_eval/wikipedia_english`, `bbc_news`, `lm_eval/mmlu_auxiliary_train` | Partial for knowledge, insufficient for abstention | AA-Omniscience public data as known-answer and unknown/abstain target variants; track answer likelihood and abstention likelihood separately |
| IFBench | Precise instruction following, formatting, counting, transformations | Existing synthetic format/numeric/table probes cover some surface constraints | Insufficient | IFBench prompt -> compliant answer target-only slice; split by constraint family |
| HLE text-only | Hard academic reasoning and knowledge | `m2d2_s2orc`, arXiv slices, `lm_eval/mmlu_auxiliary_train`, `bio_chem/*` | Partial but too indirect | HLE text-only prompt -> answer target-only slice, with subject tags |
| GPQA Diamond | Graduate-level science MCQ reasoning | arXiv physics/CS, bio/chem notation, MMLU auxiliary | Partial but too indirect | GPQA Diamond question/options -> answer letter and/or answer text target-only slice |
| CritPt | Frontier physics reasoning with code/symbolic/numeric answers | `uncheatable_eval/arxiv_physics`, formal methods, numeric-format probes | Weak partial | CritPt public challenge prompts -> expected expression/function/numeric target slices, subject to data availability |

Standalone AA text evals not in Index v4.0 but still useful surrogates:

| Eval | Current surrogate | Sufficiency | Add |
|---|---|---|---|
| MMLU-Pro | `lm_eval/mmlu_auxiliary_train` | Partial | MMLU-Pro 10-option prompted answer target-only |
| AIME 2025 | `lm_eval/gsm8k_train`, numeric-format probes | Insufficient | AIME 2025 problem -> normalized integer answer target-only |
| LiveCodeBench | Stack v2, GitHub Python, package/code slices | Partial surface only | prompt -> accepted Python solution target-only |
| Global-MMLU-Lite | FineWeb2 multilingual raw slices | Partial for language familiarity, weak for reasoning | multilingual MCQ prompt -> answer target-only for AA languages |

Suggested status labels:

- Good enough for regular tracking now: Paloma core, Uncheatable knowledge/code/science, selected FineWeb2, structured tables, MMLU/GSM8K bridge, `formal_methods/smt_lib`.
- Add next for AA surrogate quality: IFBench, GPQA Diamond, HLE text-only, MATH/AIME, SciCode/LiveCodeBench, AA-Omniscience public data.
- Keep diagnostic/archival: synthetic numeric/format probes, bio/chem notation, raw web/SVG/OCR, patch/diff/surface-form probes.

Bottom line: current Marin PPL is useful as a broad data-fit dashboard, but it is not yet a decent AA surrogate. The minimum useful upgrade is a `text_comparison_core` bundle plus supervised target-only slices for instruction following, scientific reasoning, math, and code-generation targets.

# Research

Existing perplexity-gap registry is the canonical assembly point. [`perplexity_gap_registry.py#L72-L110`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py#L72-L110) defines four bundles: `base_raw` (Paloma + Uncheatable English/code subset), `multilingual_raw` (FineWeb2 top-50 + Indic), `runnable_long_tail` (SVG-Stack, VerilogEval), and `bio_chem`. Active Paloma slices: [`paloma.py#L26-L43`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/paloma.py#L26-L43). Uncheatable ACTIVE_DATASETS (English/code only): [`exp1600_uncheatable_evals.py#L34-L59`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/exp1600_uncheatable_evals.py#L34-L59). LM-eval bridge already stages MMLU `auxiliary_train` and GSM8K `train` as raw text: [`exp5053_lm_eval_bridge.py#L71-L114`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/exp5053_lm_eval_bridge.py#L71-L114). Structured tables (totto / wikitablequestions / gittables / WebDataCommons): [`structured_evals.py#L1-L72`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/structured_evals.py#L1-L72). Formal-methods archive slices (Z3, CoqGym, VerilogEval, RTL-Repo, RTLCoder): [`formal_methods_ppl.py#L27-L33`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/formal_methods_ppl.py#L27-L33).

Generative reasoning eval names live in evalchemy (MATH500, AIME24/25/26, GPQA-Diamond, HLE, LiveCodeBench v5/v6): [`evalchemy_task_configs.py#L54-L111`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/evalchemy_task_configs.py#L54-L111). MMLU-Pro is already mirrored as eval JSON: [`eval_datasets.py#L122-L372`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/eval_datasets.py#L122-L372). None of MMLU-Pro / GPQA / HLE / MATH-500 / AIME / LiveCodeBench / SciCode / IFBench are currently exposed as **raw-text PPL targets** in any registered bundle — they exist only as pass@1 generative tasks.

**Gap vs AA axes:** Paloma+Uncheatable cover general English text + code surface form well but contain zero supervised math/reasoning targets, no MMLU-Pro/GPQA target text, no instruction-following surface, and no LiveCodeBench/SciCode prompts. The runnable long-tail bundle covers SVG and VerilogEval prompts only — not the AA-graded coding surface.

# Proposed classification and plan

Scope check: this is multi-module design + dataset onboarding work that will span at least 6–8 PRs (each new bridge = its own download + manifest + raw_text_dataset + registry wiring, see how `exp5053_lm_eval_bridge.py` did it for MMLU/GSM8K). Per AGENTS guidance and the issue's own \"file implementation issues or PRs for the chosen datasets,\" I am not opening a PR here. Below is the design pass for review.

**AA axis → existing slice mapping**

- general_knowledge: paloma `c4_en` / `wikitext_103`, uncheatable `wikipedia_english` / `bbc_news`, lm_eval `mmlu_auxiliary_train`
- scientific_reasoning: paloma `m2d2_s2orc_unsplit`, uncheatable `arxiv_physics` / `arxiv_computer_science`; **target text missing for GPQA / MMLU-Pro / SciCode**
- math: lm_eval `gsm8k_train` only; **missing MATH-500, AIME, MMLU-Pro math subset**
- coding: paloma `dolma_100_programing_languages`, uncheatable `github_python` / `github_cpp`, long_tail `verilogeval_*`; **missing LiveCodeBench prompts/solutions**
- multilingual: `multilingual_raw` bundle (FineWeb2 top-50 + Indic). Keep separate per AA methodology.
- agents / instruction_following: **not covered**; needs an IFBench target-text bridge
- long_context: **not covered**; no slice currently above the `DEFAULT_MAX_EVAL_LENGTH=4096` cap, see [`perplexity_gap_registry.py#L34-L36`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py#L34-L36)
- structured / tables: structured_evals (totto / wikitablequestions / gittables / WebDataCommons) — not yet a registered bundle, candidate for inclusion
- formal_methods: long_tail (verilogeval) and formal_methods_ppl archive (Z3 / CoqGym / RTL) — currently archival, not in regular tracking

**Proposed `text_comparison_core` bundle (cheap, regular tracking)**

Conservative: Paloma `c4_en`, `wikitext_103`, `m2d2_s2orc_unsplit`, `m2d2_wikipedia_unsplit`, `dolma_100_programing_languages`; Uncheatable `wikipedia_english`, `bbc_news`, `arxiv_physics`, `arxiv_computer_science`, `github_python`, `github_cpp`; lm_eval `mmlu_auxiliary_train`, `gsm8k_train`; structured `totto`, `wikitablequestions`, `gittables`; formal `verilogeval_canonical_solution`. This is implementable today by composing the existing factories in a new `text_comparison_core_bundle()` in `perplexity_gap_registry.py` — no new datasets required. ~17 slices, fits within `DEFAULT_MAX_DOCS_PER_DATASET=256`.

**Proposed new bridges (one sub-issue per row)**

Each follows the `exp5053_lm_eval_bridge.py` pattern: pin HF revision, declare `IngestionSourceManifest` with `UsagePolicy.EVAL_ONLY` + `contamination_risk=\"high\"`, write a renderer, expose `raw_text_dataset`. Estimated 80–200 LOC each.

- mmlu_pro_test_target: `TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro` test split, target-letter rendering. Mirror already exists at `raw/TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro`.
- gpqa_diamond_target: `Idavidrein/gpqa` diamond split, target-letter rendering. Gated dataset — confirm access.
- math500_target: `HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500`, render full solution as target.
- aime_target: AIME24/25/26 problem+solution. Source TBD (HF hosts community mirrors).
- hle_text_only_target: `cais/hle` text-only subset.
- ifbench_target: IFBench instructions + reference completions for instruction-following PPL.
- livecodebench_target: `livecodebench/code_generation_lite` v5/v6 prompts + canonical solutions.
- scicode_target: `SciCode1/SciCode` problems + solutions.
- aa_omniscience_known_unknown: TBD — AA-Omniscience-style known/unknown QA needs a source dataset decision (no obvious public mirror).

**Archival vs regular tracking recommendation**

Regular (cheap, in `text_comparison_core`): everything above plus mmlu_pro_test_target, gpqa_diamond_target, math500_target, ifbench_target, livecodebench_target once landed. These are small (≤2 MB after sample caps) and high-signal for AA axes.

Archival diagnostic only: aime_target (tiny n, high variance), scicode_target (small, niche), hle_text_only_target (saturates slowly), aa_omniscience known/unknown (until source is decided). Also archival: the bio_chem bundle, the formal_methods archive slices beyond `verilogeval_canonical_solution`, and the long-tail `web_markup` / `binary_security` / `package_metadata` / `game_music` families from [`long_tail_ppl.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/long_tail_ppl.py).

**Sub-issues to file once the above is approved**

One umbrella issue (\"Implement text_comparison_core bundle and new AA target-PPL bridges\") with the bundle wiring as the first PR, then one sub-issue per bridge above. Each sub-issue links back to #5819.

**Requesting human signoff on:**

1. The bundle membership list above (any drop/add?).
2. Whether `aa_omniscience_known_unknown` should be deferred until AA publishes a source dataset.
3. Whether the existing `runnable_long_tail` and `bio_chem` bundles should stay separate (current proposal) or be folded into archival under a renamed `archival_diagnostic` bundle.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Reframe around competencies, not benchmark names.

MMLU auxiliary_train is reasonable as a small MCQA tracking canary, but it should not be presented as an AA surrogate or allowed to dominate the core suite. AA lists MMLU-Pro as an additional text eval rather than a main Intelligence Index component, and MMLU-Pro partially overlaps the MMLU family. Use MMLU auxiliary_train as one broad-domain MCQA anchor, then diversify with other train-set/non-AA MCQA sources such as ARC-Challenge train, OpenBookQA train, CommonsenseQA train, SciQ train, QASC train, and RACE train.

Suggested competency framing:

| Competency | Why it matters for AA-like text comparisons | Candidate core PPL surrogates | Current status |
|---|---|---|---|
| MCQA competence | Broad knowledge/reasoning under answer-choice format; proxy for MMLU/GPQA/HLE-style surfaces without using their held-out items | `lm_eval/mmlu_auxiliary_train` as a canary; add ARC/OpenBookQA/CommonsenseQA/SciQ/QASC/RACE train target-only slices | Partial |
| Scientific/technical reasoning | Covers GPQA/HLE/CritPt/SciCode-adjacent science and technical prose | arXiv physics/CS, S2ORC, bio/chem notation, formal methods; add non-benchmark generated science QA from source docs | Partial |
| Math/numeric reasoning | Covers AIME/MATH-like arithmetic, algebra, answer normalization, symbolic/numeric format | GSM8K train canary, synthetic numeric-format probes; add generated math templates and open math-prose derived QA | Weak |
| Agentic coding and debugging | Covers Terminal-Bench/SciCode/LiveCodeBench-like software task surfaces | Stack v2/code ecosystem, GitHub Python/CPP, patch/diff probes, package metadata; coordinate with #4963 / #5248 for broader code/agent traces | Partial |
| Instruction following and formatting | Covers IFBench-like precise constraints, output schemas, count/transform instructions | synthetic delimiter/format/numeric probes; add generated instruction-following train slices by constraint family | Weak |
| Long-context reading and retrieval | Covers AA-LCR-like document use and answer extraction | current defaults are short; add long reports/legal/academic docs, span reconstruction, and synthetic QA over long source docs | Missing |
| Professional-document competence | Covers GDPval-AA-like workplace document/table/report outputs | structured tables, web tables, public reports/memos/spreadsheets-as-text; add document transformation and summarization target slices from non-benchmark sources | Weak-partial |
| Factuality and abstention surface | Covers AA-Omniscience-like known/unknown handling; PPL is only an indirect proxy | Wikipedia/Wikidata factual cloze, known-answer completions, synthetic unknown/abstain targets | Weak |
| Multilingual text competence | Separate from main AA English index but useful for model comparison | selected FineWeb2 languages; possibly Global-MMLU-like train-only/non-AA MCQA in major languages | Partial |
| Structured/formatted data competence | Captures tables, JSON, TSV/CSV, logs, IDs, paths; explains many PPL gaps not visible in natural text | ToTTo, WikiTableQuestions, GitTables, WebDataCommons, JSON/log/IP/SVG/patch probes | Good diagnostic coverage, decide core subset |

Proposed core principle: each competency should have 1-3 regular tracking slices, preferably from train splits or non-benchmark source distributions. Exact AA/MMLU-Pro/GPQA/HLE/AIME/LiveCodeBench/IFBench questions should stay out of core tracking unless we explicitly mark them as diagnostic and opt-in.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Correction: do not include HLE text-only, or any exact HLE items, in the PPL tracking sets.

The PPL suite needs proper validation sets that are not the actual benchmark test set. Treat HLE only as a competency signal to approximate, not as a data source. The previous mapping should be read as “HLE maps to scientific/technical reasoning + factuality + MCQA/math,” not “add HLE text-only as a slice.”

Replacement guidance:

| Competency HLE represents | Use for core PPL tracking | Do not use |
|---|---|---|
| Hard scientific/technical reasoning | arXiv/S2ORC/PubMed-derived validation text; textbook-like open science corpora; generated MCQA/short-answer from held-out source documents; formal-methods/science notation slices | HLE text-only questions/items |
| Broad difficult factual knowledge | Wikipedia/Wikidata-derived cloze or QA validation from held-out snapshots; non-AA knowledge QA train/validation sources where licensing permits | HLE items or near-duplicates |
| Math/numeric reasoning | generated math templates; open math prose-derived QA; GSM8K train as a small canary if desired | AIME/MATH/HLE test questions as core tracking |

Core rule: exact benchmark items from AA components, including HLE, GPQA, AIME, LiveCodeBench, IFBench, and similar held-out tests, should not be regular PPL tracking data. comments.author: dlwh
comments.body: @claude how do you feel about this taxonomy. Should we consider refining it?

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
**Claude finished @dlwh's task in 2m 42s** —— [View job](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/26209925142)

---
### Thoughts on the competency taxonomy

Short answer: yes, refine. The competency framing is a real improvement over "list of AA evals," but it still has some load-bearing conflations that will bite once we start picking slices and reading dashboards. Concretely:

#### 1. Surface format is being smuggled in as capability

`MCQA competence`, `Long-context reading and retrieval`, and `Structured/formatted data competence` are **surfaces**, not capabilities. They describe the shape of the input/output, not what the model has to know or infer. Treating them as competencies invites two failure modes:

- An "MCQA competence" line on the dashboard can move because the model got better at answer-letter calibration on arts MMLU while physics MCQA stays flat. Format-following improvement reads as a competency win.
- The same model can be great at long-context retrieval over legal docs and terrible at long-context math reasoning. Bundling under "long-context" hides which underlying competency is moving.

Suggest pulling surface out into its own axis (see (5) below).

#### 2. PPL fidelity is not uniform across rows, and the taxonomy is silent on this

Some competencies are well-served by raw next-token PPL. Others are not, and labelling them as PPL surrogates oversells what we can measure:

| Competency row | PPL fidelity | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Factual recall | High | Direct: does the model assign high prob to the right continuation |
| Scientific/technical prose familiarity | High | Direct: vocabulary + idiom |
| Math/numeric format | Medium | PPL on the right answer string is reasonable; PPL on derivation steps is mostly format |
| Instruction following | Low–Medium | PPL on a compliant completion doesn't separate "model would have produced this" from "model can score this likely once given" |
| Abstention/calibration | **Very low** | Raw PPL on an "I don't know" string is dominated by token frequency, not by whether the model would have abstained unprompted |
| Agentic state tracking | **Very low** | PPL over a tau2-style transcript scores trace plausibility, not the model's standalone action choice |
| Long-context retrieval | Low for retrieval, OK for reading | PPL doesn't reward locating the right span; it rewards smoothly predicting whatever comes next |

This is the most important refinement: **every competency row needs a `ppl_fidelity` tag**, and rows tagged Low/Very-low should either get a non-PPL companion metric (target-only NLL with a paired distractor, exact-match on a likelihood-argmax, calibration score, etc.) or be honestly de-listed as "PPL surrogate."

#### 3. Several competencies bundle dissociable subcapabilities

- `Factuality and abstention surface` mixes three things that empirically dissociate: **recall** (entity→attribute), **distractor discrimination** (correct vs. plausible-wrong PPL gap), and **abstention calibration** (does P("I don't know" | unanswerable) exceed P(plausible-wrong | unanswerable)). PPL is great for the first, OK for the second with paired data, near-useless for the third.
- `Agentic coding and debugging` bundles code-gen, code-read, patch/diff, and tool-trace likelihood. These pull on different slices of the training distribution and predict different downstream evals. At minimum split **code-generation surface** from **patch/diff surface** from **tool-use trace likelihood** (the last with a low-fidelity flag).
- `Structured/formatted data competence` should split into **structured input comprehension** (reading tables/JSON/logs) and **structured output generation** (producing them under constraint). AA's GDPval cares about the second; ToTTo-like slices mostly measure the first.
- `Professional-document competence` is doing a lot of work. Legal, medical/clinical, financial/SEC, scientific, technical-docs, and government/policy text have meaningfully different vocabularies and downstream sensitivity. Decompose into domain sub-rows; #5827 is already moving this way.

#### 4. Missing dimensions

- **Discrimination as a first-class metric**, not just raw PPL. For every MCQA-ish surrogate, the most predictive signal is `NLL(correct | prompt) − NLL(top-distractor | prompt)`. Without this, MCQA-format slices mostly measure prior-style features. This is also the cleanest non-PPL companion metric for abstention (paired answerable / unanswerable contrasts).
- **Dialogue / multi-turn surface** as an explicit surface (helpdesk transcripts, CRM logs, IRC/Slack-style, multi-turn QA). Currently fused into "agentic" but it's distinct: tau2 / GDPval need this even when no tool use is involved.
- **Code reading vs. code writing** (PPL on `code → docstring/explanation` is a different signal than PPL on `prompt → code`).
- **Temporal-stability tag** per slice. Some competencies will look frozen if the corpus is stale relative to AA's refresh cadence; we should know which.
- **Emergence/scaling regime tag** per slice (early / mid / late / saturates-early). Useful for picking which slices belong on the *training* dashboard vs. which only move at end-of-run.

#### 5. Proposed shape: 3-axis matrix with per-cell metadata

Replace the flat competency list with **(capability × domain × surface)**, plus tags:

- **Capability** (what the model has to do): `recall`, `inference`, `generation`, `comprehension`, `format_control`, `calibration/abstention`
- **Domain** (what it has to do it about): `general`, `science` {phys, bio, chem, cs, med}, `math`, `code`, `professional` {legal, financial, medical, technical, government}, `multilingual`
- **Surface** (how it has to read/write it): `free_form`, `mcqa`, `structured`, `dialogue`, `long_context`

Per slice, tag:
- `ppl_fidelity`: `high | medium | low | n/a` — slices marked `low`/`n/a` need a companion metric or get demoted to "diagnostic only"
- `discrimination_available`: bool — do we have paired correct/distractor for PPL-gap scoring
- `role`: `headline | diagnostic | canary` — exactly one or two headline slices per `(capability, domain)` cell, the rest diagnostic
- `scaling_regime`: `early | mid | late | saturating` — drives whether it belongs on the training dashboard

This lets you ask things like "show me all `headline` slices where `capability=inference` and `domain∈{math, science}`" without re-bundling each time AA changes its index.

#### 6. Quick wins that don't require a new design

If the larger restructure is too much right now, the cheapest high-value moves are:

1. **Add `ppl_fidelity` to every existing slice.** Forces honesty about what we're claiming.
2. **Add paired-distractor variants where possible.** For `mmlu_auxiliary_train` and `gsm8k_train` we already have the correct answer; producing a top-distractor render is cheap and unlocks the discrimination metric — the most predictive PPL-adjacent signal we have for MCQA/math.
3. **Demote MCQA from competency to surface in the bundle docstring**, even before refactoring code. Stops the dashboard-reading failure mode in (1).
4. **Split `Factuality and abstention`** into two rows now, with abstention flagged as needing non-PPL evaluation. This avoids #5826 being implicitly held to a metric it can't satisfy.
5. **In `text_comparison_core_bundle()`** (whenever it lands in `perplexity_gap_registry.py`), include the `(capability, domain, surface, ppl_fidelity, role)` tuple as bundle-side metadata so it shows up in W&B tags alongside `dataset_bundle=...` — costs nothing, makes every subsequent slicing exercise easier. The existing wandb-tags channel in `perplexity_gap_registry.py:212-217` is already the right hook.

#### What I'd keep from the current taxonomy

- The core principle of "competencies, not benchmark items" is exactly right.
- The AA task→competency mapping in the 22:12 comment is a good cross-reference and worth keeping even after the matrix refactor — it answers a different question ("if AA changed X, what should we expect to move?").
- The diagnostic/archival vs. regular-tracking split is right; tagging via `role` rather than via bundle membership is what I'd change.

#### Bottom line

The taxonomy is the right level of analysis but is roughly 60% capability and 40% surface mixed together, and it doesn't yet say which rows PPL can faithfully measure. Refactoring to a (capability × domain × surface) matrix with per-slice `ppl_fidelity`, `discrimination_available`, `role`, and `scaling_regime` tags would (a) keep the existing subissues (#5823–#5829) intact, since they map cleanly onto cells of the matrix, and (b) prevent the dashboard from accidentally tracking surface improvements as capability gains.

## Summary

This sweep investigated recurrent NaNs in `experiments/grug/parallel_attn_mlp` by running a region-pinned v6e-4 learning-rate sweep and then a larger v6e-32 confirmation. The useful result was that the default-style `lr=3e-3, warmup=1000` run stayed finite through 400 steps and beat the `2e-3` run on loss; a v6e-32 confirmation reached step 500 successfully. Further sweep breadth was blocked by repeated Iris launch kills, so the practical conclusion is that the parallel-attn-mlp path had a reproducible non-NaN setting, with infra instability limiting broader hyperparameter exploration.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/3316#issuecomment-4010637025
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/3316#issuecomment-4014263360
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description
Parallel-attn-mlp Grug runs on Nemotron mix have shown recurrent `NaN` loss behavior. We need a controlled hyperparameter sweep on `v6e-4` to find stable (non-NaN) settings before scaling back up.

## Hypothesis or Goal
Find at least one reproducible hyperparameter configuration for `experiments/grug/parallel_attn_mlp` that does not enter NaN over an initial stability window.

Success metrics:
- primary: no `NaN` in `train/loss` through at least 400 steps
- secondary: finite eval losses at first eval checkpoint
- tertiary: stable gradient norms (no `NaN` in `grad/norm/total` watch intervals)

Initial hypotheses:
- effective LR schedule is too aggressive for the parallel residual variant
- longer warmup and/or lower peak LR should prevent early numerical failure
- stronger stabilizers (`z_loss_weight`, lower `max_grad_norm`) may help if LR-only tuning is insufficient

- LR sweep (holding other vars fixed): `3e-3`, `2e-3`, `1e-3`, `5e-4`
- then warmup sweep around best LR: `1000`, `2000`, `4000`
- then stabilization sweep if needed: `z_loss_weight` and `max_grad_norm`

Fixed baseline case:
- `experiments/grug/parallel_attn_mlp/launch.py` default optimizer/trainer settings
- run on `v6e-4` so hardware stays constant during the sweep

Stop criteria:
- stop when we get at least one `replicated` non-NaN config (>=2 runs) or when all planned one-axis sweeps fail and we need architecture-level changes.

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This campaign tested whether the ragged EP64 all-to-all path could match the fixed-transport hero throughput target while keeping trained-router drops below 2% at the full 8/384 hero shape on one NVL72 rack. The drop criterion is met with large margin: the real-LR drop-trajectory run averaged 0.107% drops over steps 250-299 at cf 1.15. Throughput improved from the initial 20.20% MFU / 223k tok/s configuration to a 21.82% MFU / 241k tok/s frontier after QuACK GEMM scheduling work, with zero drops and bit-identical loss across the tuning arms. The issue's current conclusion is that the in-scope configuration and compute-tuning levers are exhausted: split counts, store width, symmetric buffers, fused device kernel, command buffers, HBM optimizer residency, GEMM tile/cluster/persistence, backward mask removal, and overlap-limit changes do not close the remaining gap. Reaching the original ~25% / ~300k tok/s target now depends on a faster structural transport path, tracked separately in marin-ep, rather than more launch-flag tuning here.

### Helpful links
- Prior ragged EP64 crash/fix campaign: #8077
- Capacity/drop analysis: #8062
- Upstream ragged all-to-all gate: https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/47283
- Configuration phase conclusion: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5305649465
- Compute-tuning frontier: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5308322722
- Final in-scope lever closure: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5309167198
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## TL;DR

Campaign start. The ragged all-to-all hero (E384, top-8, i3072, EP64 on one NVL72 rack) runs at 20.20% MFU / 223k tokens/s (`ra2a-mw-g17`, cf 1.00, LR≈0 harness). The goal is throughput comparable to the fixed-transport `moe_hero_ep` template (~25% MFU, ~300k tokens/s per rack) while holding steady-state trained-router drops under 2%.

## Description

#8077 root-caused and fixed the EP64 one-shot crash (openxla/xla#47283, kMaxPeers rebuild wheel) and validated the first ragged EP64 hero run. The ragged transport pools receiver capacity per device, so it drops far less than `fixed_all_to_all` at the same capacity factor: at cf 1.1–1.2 the trained-regime drop rate measures ≤0.05% (analytical replay of #8062 histograms; empirical r02 at EP16), versus ~4% for the fixed template at cf 1.30–1.33. What remains is a throughput gap.

Reference points at hero scale on one rack: fixed transport at iso-active-compute (`mhep-baseline-e192k4-i6144-cf133-fp32-20260814-c`) reaches 23.6% MFU / 251k tokens/s at ~3.9% drops; the half-active-compute reference (`mhep-baseline-e192k4-cf133-fp32-20260814-b`, i3072) reaches 25.3% / 346k.

Constraints: no model change, and no quantization beyond what `moe_hero_ep` on main already performs (per the [fidelity discussion](https://openathena.slack.com/archives/C0AHF5KV11Q/p1786740832465729?thread_ts=1786583521.652629&cid=C0AHF5KV11Q)). The ragged training path is currently bf16 end to end.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Reach ~25% MFU / ~300k tokens/s at the full hero shape (d6144/L48, E384, top-8, i3072, latent 3072, batch 1024) on one NVL72 rack with the ragged transport, then demonstrate <2% steady-state drops at the chosen capacity posture and loss parity against the existing EP implementation via `small_scale_abl_launch.py`.

## Status

h01 (cf 1.15 posture baseline) and h02 (latency-hiding scheduler + overlap limit 4, retesting the safe-flag retreat adopted on the broken barrier generation) are running. Queued: splits-per-peer sweep at EP64, command buffers at the #8277 capture set, XProf anatomy of the best configuration.

🤖 Transport-lever update. The splits ladder is sealed (16 worse, 32≈64 tied at 20.0% MFU) and 16-byte stores in the symmetric kernel are flat (h08, 20.12%), so the residual 4.0 s/step transport cost is structural to the symmetric-kernel-plus-external-barriers path.

The promising alternative is upstream's newer fused one-shot (`--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel`): one kernel per collective, 512 threads/CTA, 16-byte vectors, in-kernel NCCL LSA barrier. A 4-node probe (`ra2a-mw-h10-ep16-e48-devkernel-vlog-20260815`) shows it engages and then dies on exactly the openxla/xla#47146 gate: `RET_CHECK failure (ragged_all_to_all_thunk.cc:943) peer_access_enabled` — a CUDA-P2P check that the NVL72 window mapping does not need (the symmetric kernel already does cross-node `ncclGetLsaPointer` writes in every passing run). issues.author: RohithKuditipudi
issues.body:
A caller that runs `execute()` on a worker thread has no way, from any other thread, to make it stop early — whether the pipeline's results are no longer needed or the process is shutting down. If the worker job that `execute()` launches never schedules (no accelerator capacity), the call blocks for 12 hours and nothing can release it sooner.

What `execute()` launches: on a fresh context it calls `_start_pool()`, which submits a coordinator job (`execution.py:502`), tells it to spawn a worker job, and waits for the first worker to register — up to `ZEPHYR_WORKERS_READY_WAIT`, default 12 h (`execution.py:532-533`). The handles to these jobs are held in variables local to the call (`execution.py:646`); nothing is assigned to the context object, and `self._state` stays `NEW`.

What `shutdown()` does: it stops what the context has registered — the pool that only `start()` assigns (`execution.py:550`) — and returns immediately for state `NEW` (`execution.py:689`). During `execute()` it therefore has no effect: the jobs it would need to stop are reachable only from inside the blocked call. Calling `start()` first does not help: `start()` holds `_state_lock` across the same first-worker wait (`execution.py:550`), and `shutdown()` blocks acquiring that lock (`execution.py:684`).

What changed: before #7145, `execute()` stored its coordinator job on the instance (`self._coordinator_job`) and `shutdown()` terminated that job — workers included, via cascading termination — from any thread at any point in the call. #7145 moved the pool into the `execute()` call and rewrote `shutdown()` around the `NEW`/`OWNER` state machine; cancelling a running `execute()` was dropped with no replacement.

Observed in production, 2026-08-22/23: a driver needed to cancel `execute()` calls whose work other pools had already completed. The v5litepod worker jobs never scheduled (`Insufficient TPUs (need 4, available 0)`); `shutdown()` at ~02:00 UTC had no effect, and each blocked call held its thread until the 12 h wait expired at ~11:20 UTC. The only unstick was killing the coordinator jobs out-of-band.

Done when: `shutdown()` (or an equivalent) promptly cancels a running `execute()`, including one still waiting for its first worker. One shape: register the coordinator group on the context at creation, before the blocking waits; deregister when the pool ends; have `shutdown()` stop registered live groups regardless of state.

## TL;DR

We ran a 48-cell controlled ablation over three task sources, two frontier teachers, two agent harnesses, 32k and 131k contexts, and summarization on or off. Every cell cleared the 90% infrastructure-success gate. Terminus-2 had a clear paired advantage in 17 of 24 harness comparisons; OpenCode had a clear advantage in 3, all for GLM-5.2 on OpenSWE, and 4 were inconclusive. The largest failure was HCSA-025: OpenCode entered a repeated auto-compaction loop, produced 25,119 compaction events, and fell from 68.33% reward in the compaction-off control to 27.67%.

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
The GB200 EP hero run (704 processes, 11 racks) fails with `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` on a single contiguous allocation inside `jit_train_step`. One process dies, enters the JAX shutdown barrier alone, and after the ~5 minute barrier deadline the coordination service propagates a fatal error to all 704 ranks. This happened 8 times on 2026-08-20 across four configurations.

The allocation is XLA's `preallocated-temp` arena, one contiguous buffer for the whole step. From a one-rack buffer-assignment dump (`expert_axis_size` is fixed at 64 and racks are data-parallel replicas, so per-device shapes match the 11-rack run):

```
allocation 3216: size 137,430,636,656 (127.99 GiB), preallocated-temp
  36.00 GiB  bf16[48,16,4096,6144]     per-layer activation save-stack
  40.50 GiB  f32[48,6,3072,3072] x 4   offloaded optimizer state staged back on device
```

731 GiB of HLO values pack into that 128 GiB arena (5.7x live-range reuse), so the arena is a liveness peak rather than a sum of buffers.

Representative failure, with `--xla_gpu_memory_limit_slop_factor=88` and `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.75`:

```
cuMemAllocAsync failed to allocate 126,257,359,472 bytes (117.59 GiB)
Free memory/Total:      18,801,229,824 / 197,890,015,232
Limit: 138.22 GiB   MaxInUse: 135.64 GiB
CU_MEMPOOL_ATTR_RESERVED_MEM_CURRENT: 148,411,252,736  (138.22 GiB)
CU_MEMPOOL_ATTR_USED_MEM_CURRENT:      19,381,558,256  ( 18.05 GiB)
```

Free space inside the pool was 120.17 GiB against a 117.59 GiB request, with another 17.51 GiB free on the device. The allocation failed with roughly 20 GiB of headroom available, so total memory is not the constraint.

| config | limit | step peak | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MEM_FRACTION=0.75` (default) | 138.22 GiB | 143.72 GiB | ~1400 steps, OOM every 31 min to 3.5 h, 43% wall-clock efficiency |
| `MEM_FRACTION=0.83` (#8490) | 152.97 GiB | 143.72 GiB | 3 OOMs in 70 min; never resumed training after the restore; device free fell to 3.03 GB |
| `slop_factor=88`, `0.75` | 138.22 GiB | 135.64 GiB | arena shrank to 117.59 GiB; OOM ~40 s after the first step |

On reading step counts: W&B drops steps at or below a resumed run's high-water mark, so a restart that re-does completed steps logs nothing even while it trains. The 0.83 row above is based on tqdm rates rather than W&B. That run restored from `step-1389` and never produced a `rate:<N>s/it` reading in 13,426 log lines over 70 minutes; every rate was 6-9 it/s, which is the progress bar advancing to the restored position at about 150 ms per iteration. Training runs at roughly 18.4 s/step.

The working model does not explain these results. #8490 assumed that a step peak above the pool release threshold forces the pool to unmap and re-form the arena every step, so bringing peak below the threshold should help. The opposite happened. The default configuration requested 125.67 GiB against 120.17 GiB of free pool space, so it had to expand the pool on every step, and it ran for hours. The `slop=88` configuration requests less than the free pool space and fails within a minute. We do not have an explanation for that inversion.

One untested hypothesis: `cudaMallocAsync` may take different paths depending on whether a request fits in existing free pool space. A request that does not fit maps fresh backing from the driver, which is contiguous by construction. A request that does fit may be served from the pool's fragmented free list without falling back to expansion. If that holds, shrinking the arena is not monotonically helpful.

Debugging note: Iris records the wrong originating task. The recorded failure is usually the process hosting the JAX coordination service, which reports the barrier timeout. The process that actually OOMed is named in the rank-0 log as `The first task at the barrier: N`, maps to task `N // 4` at 4 GPUs per task, and is filed as `COSCHED_FAILED`. Across the seven crashes traced this way, the recorded task never matched the true originator, and the true originators were on seven different nodes. Node-frequency queries over the recorded task point at whichever node hosts task 0 and are misleading.

Every mechanism proposed so far is inferred from the allocator dump at the moment of failure. There is no time series of pool state during normal operation. `memory/peak_gib`, `memory/in_use_gib`, and `memory/limit_gib` are logged per step; the pool attributes and `cudaMemGetInfo` are not.

#8506 carries the running status log of interventions. #8507 is the change currently under test.

Done when: the run sustains training at rack scale without OOM, and the allocator behavior that causes the failure is measured rather than inferred.

Suggested next steps:

- Log `CU_MEMPOOL_ATTR_RESERVED_MEM_CURRENT`, `CU_MEMPOOL_ATTR_USED_MEM_CURRENT`, `cudaMemGetInfo` free, and `largest_free_block` per step. This rides an existing restart at no cluster cost and discriminates the hypotheses above.
- Reduce the arena instead of redistributing space around it. The optimizer update stages all 48 layers of f32 master params and moments at once, via `_tree_to_memory_kind(state.opt_state, "device")` over the whole pytree in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py`. Chunking per expert wave would free about 27 GiB. `optax.clip_by_global_norm` in the optimizer chain has to be hoisted out first, since a sliced update would otherwise compute a chunk-local norm.
- Measure the non-XLA footprint (28.5 GiB of CUDA context, NCCL, and cuBLAS/cuDNN workspaces). It is a third of the device budget and has not been examined.

Arena size is verifiable from a compile alone (`XLA_FLAGS=--xla_dump_to=...`, then the `preallocated-temp` line of `buffer-assignment.txt`), which is much cheaper than a hero relaunch for screening candidate configurations.

🤖 Ran the original configuration (slop factor at its 95 default, `MEM_FRACTION=0.75`) on one rack for 500 steps, with per-step CUDA mempool counters added to `log_device_memory`. `dp_racks=1`, `batch_size=1024`, so per-device shapes match the 11-rack run. **The pool trims to the release threshold after every step and re-acquires the arena's backing on the next one.** This was previously inferred from failure-time dumps. It is now measured directly, and held for all 500 steps:

```
mem/pool_reserved_gib        138.219   between every step (= the 0.75 threshold)
mem/pool_reserved_high_gib   147.375   high-water mark
```

The TPU canary training task fails before step 0 on every attempt while resuming a temporary checkpoint. All four task attempts raise `rigging.filesystem.cross_region.TransferBudgetExceeded`, the job exceeds `max_task_failures`, and the ferry fails.

Time-policy *temporary* checkpoints are written to a region-local temp bucket (`CheckpointerConfig.temporary_base_path` -> `gs://marin-us-central2/tmp/ttl=14d/checkpoints-temp/...`), and the resume search path appends it (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py:926`), so a restart resumes from it. The canary deliberately spreads across TPU pools in several regions for capacity -- `v5p-8` us-central1/us-east5, `v6e-4` europe-west4, `v4-8` us-central2 (`experiments/ferries/canary_ferry.py:128`). An earlier execution of this run ran in us-central2 (the only region that writes to that region-local temp bucket) and left a 23 GB temporary checkpoint at `step-30`. After preemption, all four retries rescheduled onto europe-west4 and us-central1 workers and resumed that checkpoint. Reading 23 GB from us-central2 into another region is a cross-region GCS read; the cumulative read hits the 10 GB `TransferBudget` guard (`lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem/cross_region.py:31`) and aborts before step 0.

This is the checkpoint-resume analogue of #8445 (cross-region read of the tokenized data cache), which was fixed for the canary by localizing the ~21 MB FineWeb cache through `mirror://`. The checkpoint-resume path does not go through `mirror://`, so the same guard now trips on the temporary checkpoint instead.

- attempt 0 -- `v6e-4` europe-west4 -- `TransferBudgetExceeded`
- attempts 1-3 -- `v5p-8` us-central1 -- `TransferBudgetExceeded`

Expected: a cross-region reschedule resumes the temporary checkpoint through region-local resolution (`mirror://`, matching the data cache fix) or starts fresh, rather than failing the task on the transfer guard. A short smoke canary arguably should not resume temporary checkpoints at all.

# Research

`run_grug_moe_trial()` leaves `TrainerConfig.load_checkpoint` at `None`, so Grug searches both configured checkpoint roots and reads the newest temporary checkpoint after a retry moves regions. `restore_grug_state_from_checkpoint()` already treats `False` as a hard opt-out before checkpoint discovery; no open PR overlaps #8595, and #8136 is the broader transfer-guard issue.

**Relevant code**

- [`launch.py#L146-L170`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/launch.py#L146-L170) - trainer configuration
- [`canary_ferry.py#L291-L311`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/ferries/canary_ferry.py#L291-L311) - canary launch configuration
- [`checkpointing.py#L105-L122`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/checkpointing.py#L105-L122) - resume opt-out
- [`trainer.py#L910-L929`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L910-L929) - default checkpoint search roots

# Proposed Fix

Expose the existing `load_checkpoint` setting through `GrugMoeLaunchConfig`, pass it to `TrainerConfig`, and set it to `False` for the canary. issues.author: muchanem
issues.body:
Relevant work: #6521, [MATES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06046), [Group-MATES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14709), [RegMix](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01492v2), [RegMix-D](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18663), [Meta-rater](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14194), [DataMan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.19363), [Scalable Influence and Fact Tracing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17413), [DoGE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15393v2)

tl;dr: We should label our data on a bunch of axes (downstream performance, LLM oracle, gradient alignment, etc) and cluster over those axes (and domain) to create buckets for the data mixing swarms

The literature on pre-training data selection has moved fairly significantly beyond FineWeb-Edu style pipelines where you use an LLM-as-judge to rate a sample set of your pretraining data and then train a small model to predict those scalar labels across your pretraining data. 

The first and most important change is treating quality as a multi-dimensional label. In DataMan 14 quality criteria and 15 domains labels are used; in Meta-rater data is labeled on professionalism, readability, reasoning, and cleanliness and proxy models are trained to learn the most useful combination of the signals for validation loss. A scale-up of this approach looks like [propella-1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12414v1)--Qwen3 models which produce structured JSON over 18 properties in six categories. 

The second change is moving to approaches that don't rely on an LLM oracle like downstream performance or gradient alignment. This changes include the further insight that these labels are dynamic (treating each label as conditional on training state/progress). For instance, MATES calculates loss of a model at step t after training on candidate points. DoGE calculates a gradient alignment for full domain buckets.

New work on pretraining data selection has also emphasized the importance of diversity and group-level view of utility. Group-MATES shows that the influence scores of documents cannot be considered independently, and groups documents using their individual influence scores. [Spokes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15216) emphasizes the importance of diversity as a set-level attribute, meaning that buckets themselves should likely get labels as well.

The goal then is a vector of labels per training document, which then get clustered into groups, which can be selected over by our swarms.

Our particular setting and fusing the prior work into one pipeline introduces a few questions but also resolves a few difficulties:
* We are only trying to produce buckets: Meta-rater and Group-MATES think about both the labels and how to select over the labels, we only need to produce the most informative labels possible
* We will/do have training trajectories from model trained over substantially similar data to (presumably) what we will train on in the future. This potentially gives us more signal for model-based labels. However, naively using our checkpoints introduces the danger of only incorporating a memorization/exposure signal rather than a data property itself
* Should our clusters be independent of domain or include domain as another label? (my prior is domain should be included to create clusters)
* The cost and "unity" of the labeler:
   * We could do something like propella-1 where we have a fairly large model predict our entire vector at once. However, this means we introduce a large global barrier into quality labeling work: we can get labels once all have been finalized and the labeler is trained<sup>*</sup>. Additionally, we introduce ~5,000 B200-GPU hours of cost (1B labeler, FP4) to label our training set
   * Alternatively, we train models for each axis we care about at ~the size of our current quality labeler (40M). This allows work on axes to not block each other, but at 20 axes (pessimistically 12 due to small model MFUs) we end up using the same number of GPU hours, for a presumably worse result than predicting all axes at once with a larger model


\* Something like training LoRAs per axis and folding them into the model as we add new axes could work as we expand our set of labels, but also means introducing additional risk as we are stacking multiple bets at once when moving to this approach

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body: As a straw man, what info would you think this would capture that we can't capture from an affine projection from the embeddings we have from Harrier?

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body: A lot of the information is probably directly linearly decodable from the embeddings and doesn't require training a separate model (e.g. for the quality labels, like 90% of the performance of our current model can be captured by a linear probe on the document embedding). But, it's important that the projection be learned--the dominant variance in the embeddings is topic/genre, and so clustering on the embeddings directly (or after a random projection) wouldn't recover things like the MATES downstream performance metric or gradient alignment. So the labels can be understood as making the axes we care about dominant under the clustering metric rather than averaged out. I do also suspect some axes may also turn out to have no signal above label noise in Harrier at all, so we would need to train a separate model.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
Sounds good! Yeah, I think the baseline would be to try your workflow for quality on other axes we care about and only expand to a custom model for axes we have high confidence & evidence will lead to improvements.

The fact that the expensive compute isn't re-usable is what I don't like about the Propella approach. If every time you want to add a new axis you need to re-run a full Qwen model pass over all your data, you'll quickly find yourself avoiding adding new axes because it's expensive and we're unlikely to get the axes right from the get go!

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
I am not well-read in datamixing literature and what actually works- but just a general thought on optimization.

In any open-ended optimization problem, a big decision is how to coalesce the search space into a tractable number of degrees of freedom (EG should we have a learning rate per parameter, or one global LR, or a learning rate per parameter per step). 

To me, every degree of freedom is inherently a bad thing. It exponentially grows the search space, increases risk of overfitting, and makes it harder to interpret results. And it is only worth including a degree of freedom when it empirically proves its worth. I also find it easy to underestimate the future inertia that degrees of freedom introduce. (EG if we fit a unique LR to MLP up projection, suddenly moving to Latent MoE means there is a lot more work to do to retune).

On DataMan 14 quality criteria, my first thought would be "how many of these can we remove without significantly hurting performance". I think its great to test a very large number of hypothesis during exploration phase, but afterwards, every degree of freedom of the system should be sensitive to the objective function- otherwise it should be pruned. I think its easy to get into the reverse mindset, where degrees of freedom are viewed as implying sophistication of the system (but I think this is backwards).

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
The expert-parallel ring MoE backend (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py`, `_moe_mlp_ep_ring_local`) computes wrong outputs. Against an exact fp32 dense MoE reference on a GB200 node with mesh `(data=2, expert=2, model=1)`, E=8 experts (4 per shard), top-2, 64 tokens/device, H=64, I=96, bf16, capacity factor 2.0 (both implementations report zero drops), ring's forward deviates by 0.75x-0.93x relative on most seeds and produced values of magnitude 2.3e28 on one seed; its gradients contain NaN. The ragged all-to-all backend on identical inputs matches the dense reference to 0.4-0.5% (bf16 noise) with clean gradients, so the harness and inputs are not the cause. This matters because ring is the implementation other backends are validated against (`test_moe_mlp_ragged_matches_ring_with_ep_axis_when_available` skips on CPU, so the EP path is effectively untested in CI).

A second defect: at capacity factor 4.0 in the same configuration, `jax.lax.top_k(selection_key, local_capacity)` at `ep_ring.py:88` requests k=512 from a 256-row selection pool and crashes; `local_capacity` is not capped at the gathered pool size.

Reproduce:
1. On branch `research/mcwitt/8317-ragged-tune`, submit `python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.ragged_ep_check --version dev --run` (needs 4 GB200s; the check compares ring, ragged, and the exact dense reference).
2. Read `ring_vs_dense` in the `ragged_ep_seed` log lines.

Expected: ring matches the dense fp32 reference within bf16 tolerance at a capacity factor where nothing drops, at any mesh shape.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

I reproduced both defects on current `main` with four GB200s. At capacity 2.0, ring had 0 drops but forward relative max error was 0.79, 0.90, 0.96, and 1.93 across seeds 0–3; seed 1 produced non-finite gradients. Forcing `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=xla` reduced those errors to 0.005–0.007 with finite gradients, isolating the corruption to the Triton ragged-dot kernel: its physical power-of-two tiles read and write past logical M/N/K boundaries. Capacity 4.0 separately requests `top_k(k=512)` from 256 rows.

**Relevant code**
- [`ragged_dot.py#L103-L135`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L103-L135) - unmasked forward tiles
- [`ragged_dot.py#L179-L210`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L179-L210) - unmasked weight-gradient tiles
- [`ep_ring.py#L56-L88`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py#L56-L88) - uncapped selection capacity
- [`test_grugformer_moe.py#L957-L1012`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/tests/grug/test_grugformer_moe.py#L957-L1012) - ring used as oracle

# Proposed Fix

Mask edge reads and writes in both Triton ragged-dot layouts, and cap ring's selection capacity at the gathered assignment pool size. Replace ring-as-oracle coverage with value and gradient comparisons against a direct dense `einsum` MoE reference; retain backend-to-backend checks only as secondary diagnostics. Exercise ring at excess capacity to cover the crash, and validate the portable ring, ragged all-to-all, fixed all-to-all, and pooled-wave paths against the dense reference where their runtimes are available.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body: 🤖 Draft fix: #8610. Masking logical Triton tile boundaries reduced ring's four-seed GB200 forward error from 0.79–1.93 to 0.005–0.007, restored finite gradients within 0.006 of the fp32 dense reference, and made capacity factor 4.0 succeed. spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This probe compared upstream-shaped FlashAttention-4 THD/varlen attention against Marin's current Grug segmented FA4/CuTe path on B200 for the exact d5120 Grug causal attention shape. The measured THD compact `cu_seqlens` path was materially faster than the current segmented FA4/CuTe implementation across the tested packed layouts, but the usable prototype is still a torch/DLPack bridge rather than a JIT-safe JAX FFI. The recommended integration direction is fixed max-segment metadata plus a real THD/JAX FFI path, while avoiding the private JAX cuDNN packed-offset path until its exact-GQA numerics are validated.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/issue5815-fa4-thd-logbook-20260529/.agents/logbooks/issue5815-fa4-thd.md
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6059
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Issue5815 needs a narrow benchmark of upstream-shaped FlashAttention-4 THD/varlen attention against the current Grug dense BSHD segmented FA4/CuTe port on B200. The target shape is the exact d5120 Grug causal self-attention q/k/v layout: q `[B,S,Hq,D]`, k/v `[B,S,Hkv,D]`.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Determine whether reshaping BSHD to THD, building `cu_seqlens` from packed segment IDs or fixed segment metadata, and calling upstream FA4 CuTe varlen materially beats the current segmented FA4 path for fwd+bwd. Thresholds: `<=0.005s` promising, `0.005-0.010s` marginal, `>0.010s` not worth pursuing for issue5815.

### Links

* Stable research tag: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/issue5815-fa4-thd-logbook-20260529
* Stable research logbook: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/issue5815-fa4-thd-logbook-20260529/.agents/logbooks/issue5815-fa4-thd.md
* Stable probe script: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/issue5815-fa4-thd-logbook-20260529/scratch/issue5815_attention_backend_probe.py
* Draft PR: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6059
* Code paths: `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py`, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py`, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_thd.py`

## Results

Latest focused B200 probe for exact d5120, `S=4096,Hq=40,Hkv=8,D=128`, dynamic uneven segments:

| segs/row | B | dense upstream | current FA4/CuTe | THD fixed lengths | THD compact cu-lens |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 1 | 0.000681s | 0.001939s | 0.000892s | 0.000656s |
| 2 | 4 | 0.002399s | 0.006653s | 0.002391s | 0.002151s |
| 4 | 1 | 0.000680s | 0.001280s | 0.000790s | 0.000561s |
| 4 | 4 | 0.002343s | 0.004249s | 0.002028s | 0.001801s |

## Decision log

* 2026-05-29: The public upstream PyTorch varlen wrapper alone was not enough; internal upstream FA4 `_flash_attn_fwd/_flash_attn_bwd` is the relevant API for the THD/cu-lens core.
* 2026-05-29: Fixed max-segment metadata is a useful integration point. It is materially faster than current segmented FA4/CuTe and avoids scanning full `[B,S]` segment IDs in the attention hot path.
* 2026-05-29: Do not use the private JAX cuDNN packed-offset path for exact Grug GQA until its GQA numerics are validated.

## Negative results index

* Public `flash_attn_varlen_func` autograd was slower than the internal upstream fwd/bwd API.
* Private JAX cuDNN packed offsets were fast but failed numerics for exact `Hq=40,Hkv=8` GQA.
* Including full dynamic `segment_ids -> cu_seqlens` construction inside the timed helper can erase the THD kernel win on small cases.

## Current baseline

Shape `B in {1,4} S=4096 Hq=40 Hkv=8 D=128`, bf16, causal fwd+bwd, dynamic uneven contiguous segments. Latest focused medians are listed in Results.

Design change — write before coding because the THD path does not exist.

Step 1: Add `fa4_thd_core` entry. New function in `_fa4_cute.py` that takes BSHD `q/k/v` plus `segment_ids`, reshapes BSHD → THD (`q: [B*S, Hq, D]`), and either (a) calls upstream `flash_attn.cute` varlen forward/backward directly with `cu_seqlens_q = jnp.arange(B+1, dtype=jnp.int32) * S` and `max_seqlen_q = S` — single-sequence-per-row, so the layout matches what the issue specifies — or (b) wires a thin JAX FFI wrapper around the CuTe varlen entry. Option (a) is preferred for the probe; (b) only if upstream lacks a JAX-callable handle.

Step 2: Add `jax_cudnn_core` reference. Wrap `jax.nn.dot_product_attention(..., implementation="cudnn")` with the same BSHD-in / BSHD-out signature so the three paths are directly comparable. jax cuDNN does not natively take packed segment_ids; for the probe use `is_causal=True` on the single-sequence-per-batch-row layout the issue defines.

Step 3: Write `scratch/issue5815_attention_backend_probe.py`. Driver that builds the d5120 Grug shape (issue does not pin `B/S/Hq/Hkv/D` — confirm with #5815; #5896 used `B=1, S=8192, Hq=32, Hkv=8, D=128`), runs each of `jax_cudnn_core`, `fa4_cute_core`, `fa4_thd_core` for fwd and fwd+bwd with a fixed `warmup=3, steps=10` loop, and prints steady-state ms plus value/grad max-abs vs a small-seq reference. Match the format used in the #5896 logbook so the result is appendable.

Step 4: Run on B200 (Slurm), apply the decision rule from the issue (`<=0.005s` promising / `0.005-0.010s` marginal / `>0.010s` skip) to fwd+bwd steady, and post the structured result back here.

Open questions to confirm before implementation:
- Target shape: take #5896 `(B=1,S=8192,Hq=32,Hkv=8,D=128)` or a different d5120 spec from #5815?
- Should `fa4_thd_core` call upstream `flash_attn.cute` varlen directly, or land a JAX FFI wrapper in `_fa4_cute_backend.py`?

spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment tested whether routed expert MuonH parameters in the May Grug MoE recipe should use a different learning-rate scale because each expert only sees a sparse subset of tokens. Gate 1 compared three normalizations: shrinking only routed expert LR by sqrt(sparsity), boosting the dense/non-expert MuonH LR, and a mid-ratio compromise. `boost-nonexpert` and `shrink-expert` both failed gate 1, while `mid-ratio` passed with modest effective speedups at d512 and d768, so gate 2 was launched for d1024 and d1280. The larger gate-2 run was still in recovery/monitoring in the latest issue updates, with most follow-up work focused on TPU preemptions, regional checkpoint restore, host RAM, and launcher fixes rather than a final gate-2 decision.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5799#issuecomment-4474840407
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5799#issuecomment-4477551329
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5799#issuecomment-4480453273
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## TL;DR

Test whether routed expert MuonH weights should use a smaller LR because each expert sees only a sparse fraction of tokens. Gate 1 compares two normalizations at d512 and d768 against the MoE effective-speedup gates.

## Original prompt

> I want to test the following idea on the per-expert learning rate, the per expert learning rate should be smaller as each expert see less token. My guess is that we should shrink the per-expert learning rate down by \sqrt{sparsity} (assuming sparsity is between [0,1]). On top of this idea, there are two potential candidate: we can either keep the learning rate on the remaining muonh parameters the same and decrease the per-expert learning rate; or keep the per-expert learning rate the same and increase the remaining learning rate. Let's try to do gate 1 for both and potentially do gate 2 if either pass gate1.

## Scope

Builds on #5763 (`may_arch + GN->MuonH + 1% warmup + no grad-clip`) and keeps that recipe fixed except for the MuonH LR split.

For may_arch, `num_experts_per_token=4` and `num_experts=256`, so `sparsity = 4 / 256 = 1/64` and `sqrt(sparsity) = 0.125`.

Gate-1 candidates:

| candidate | routed expert MuonH LR | remaining MuonH LR | Adam/AdamH groups |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| shrink-expert | 0.125x heuristic | 1.0x heuristic | unchanged |
| boost-nonexpert | 1.0x heuristic | 8.0x heuristic | unchanged |

Only routed expert MLP weights are in the `muonh_expert` bucket. Shared expert weights, attention matrices, and GatedNorm weights stay in the remaining MuonH bucket because they see dense traffic.

## Gate plan

Gate 1:
- d512 at 2.19e17 FLOPs
- d768 at 1.70e18 FLOPs

If either candidate shows effective speedup at both scales, run gate 2 for that candidate at:
- d1024 at 9.00e18 FLOPs
- d1280 at 2.83e19 FLOPs

## Links

- Branch: `moe_muonh_may_arch_per_expert_lr_gate1`
- Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe/muonh_may_arch_per_expert_lr_gate1.py`
- Research logbook: `.agents/logbooks/moe_per_expert_lr_sqrt_sparsity.md`

## Decision log

| Date | Decision | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-05-17 | Start with gate 1 only for both normalizations. | This isolates the LR normalization question before spending d1024/d1280 compute. |

## Negative results index

None yet.

## Current baseline

Use `experiments/grug/moe/README.md` compute-optimal baseline and `experiments/grug/moe/agent.md` effective-speedup gate definitions.

spillover_issues.author: yonromai
spillover_issues.body:
The inference dashboard does not report request-level TPOT. It queries `time_per_output_token_seconds_{bucket,count,sum}`, while pinned GPU and TPU vLLM versions and live Marin telemetry expose `request_time_per_output_token_seconds_{bucket,count,sum}`. The existing `tpot` rows instead contain inter-token latency, which is a different distribution.

Reproduce:
1. Open the inference dashboard for a serve that emits both latency families.
2. Inspect the latency rows.

Expected: report request-level TPOT and inter-token latency as separate latency families.

<details>
<summary>Supporting evidence</summary>

- [The dashboard maps both source names to `tpot`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ebba6d565b4e9dfd3e11b60cf22e8936737f804e/infra/grafana/src/vllm_observability.py#L68-L74), but the unprefixed request family is not emitted by the pinned vLLM versions.
- Live `telemetry_v1` data contains the request-prefixed histogram components and no unprefixed counterparts.
- [The latency fixture covers only inter-token latency](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ebba6d565b4e9dfd3e11b60cf22e8936737f804e/infra/grafana/tests/test_vllm_observability.py#L208-L212).
- Request TPOT contributes one mean decode time per completed request. Inter-token latency measures gaps between emitted tokens.

</details>

spillover_issues.author: yonromai
spillover_issues.body:
Echo's existing CI/CD deployment path fails at `command:local:Command migrate`. The running API and sync job are healthy, but every Echo deployment ends red and leaves the migration command pending. Pulumi can update independent resources before this command fails, so a schema-dependent release could deploy application changes without completing its migration.

Reproduce:
1. Run `Ops - Pulumi Rollout` from `main` with `service=echo` under the normal GitHub Actions identity.
2. In `Apply Pulumi stack`, observe the `migrate` command fail while acquiring impersonated credentials:

   ```text
   USER_PROJECT_DENIED: Caller does not have required permission to use project hai-gcp-models.
   Grant roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageConsumer or serviceusage.services.use.
   ```

Expected: The standard Echo rollout completes its migration and exits successfully under the CD identity.

[`migrate.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0665bfca75b1968fa86f69c7cfcafd67ee57bb98/infra/echo/migrate.py#L61) pins `hai-gcp-models` as the Cloud SQL Connector quota project. The deployment identity, `marin-cd-cloud-run-deploy@hai-gcp-models.iam.gserviceaccount.com`, does not have `serviceusage.services.use`. The durable grant belongs in Marin's [canonical project IAM configuration](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0665bfca75b1968fa86f69c7cfcafd67ee57bb98/infra/pulumi/src/iac/gcp/iam_data.yaml).

<details>
<summary>Observed failures and completion check</summary>

- The [August 23 Echo rollout](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/32667634884) failed with this diagnostic even though no new migration was added.
- The [PR #8448 merge rollout](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/32435482456) failed the same way after updating Echo resources.
- The failure also occurred in three earlier Echo rollout runs on August 12, 14, and 18.
- After applying the IAM change, dispatch the Echo rollout from current `main` and confirm that the migration completes and both Cloud Run resources remain Ready.
- This repair does not require an index rebuild or changes to Echo's application, migration, scheduler, or workflow logic.

</details>

**Relevant code**

- [`migrate.py#L61`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0665bfca75b1968fa86f69c7cfcafd67ee57bb98/infra/echo/migrate.py#L61) — selects the quota project.
